title: Ezekiel 27:1–11
context: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet, addressed as “son of man,” with a command to take up a lamentation over Tyre (27:1–3), the Phoenician port that boasted, “I am perfect in beauty.” The lament pictures the city as a splendid merchant ship built from the finest materials of the eastern Mediterranean world: planks of cypress from Senir, a cedar mast from Lebanon, oars from the oaks of Bashan, and a sail of embroidered linen from Egypt (27:4–7). Crews and craftsmen come from neighboring Phoenician cities, and soldiers from distant lands hang their shields on its walls (27:8–11). Many of the place names can be identified only tentatively. The lament follows the oracle of 26:1–21, where the LORD announces that he will bring Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon against Tyre (26:7), and it leads into the merchant list of 27:12–25 and the shipwreck of 27:26–36. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: the LORD exposes the pride of a wealthy, self-admiring power, and the beauty that Tyre credited to itself becomes the measure of its fall.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came again to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The formula marks a new message in the series of oracles against the nations (chapters 25–32), and the prophet reports it in the first person. Arminian readers note that the LORD speaks about nations beyond Israel, holding Tyre accountable for its conduct and showing that his rule reaches the whole world of trade and politics.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same formula as a sign that the message comes from the LORD rather than from the prophet’s own reflection, and they hear his sovereignty over the nations in the series as a whole. Shared ground: both traditions read the oracles against Tyre as the LORD’s word, delivered through a prophet among the exiles.

verses.text: “You, son of man, take up a lamentation over Tyre;
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet, addressed as “son of man,” is told to “take up a lamentation over Tyre.” A lament was a funeral song, and here it is raised over a city still standing. Arminian readers hear the LORD announcing judgment while it can still be heard as a warning, and they note the tone of grief rather than gloating.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear a lament that announces what the LORD has determined, sung in advance as if the funeral had already come. Shared ground: both traditions read the title “son of man” as marking the prophet’s human standing before God, and both see the dirge form as a solemn word about the end of human pride.

verses.text: and tell Tyre, ‘You who dwell at the entry of the sea, who are the merchant of the peoples to many islands, the Lord GOD says: “You, Tyre, have said, ‘I am perfect in beauty.’
verses.arminianNotes: Tyre is addressed as the one “who dwell at the entry of the sea” and “the merchant of the peoples to many islands,” and its boast is quoted: “I am perfect in beauty.” Arminian readers see a city that interpreted its success as its own achievement, and they hear the LORD confronting a self-assessment that left no room for gratitude or accountability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the boast the root of the coming judgment: a heart that ascribes to itself what belongs to God (compare Daniel 4:30). Shared ground: both traditions see pride, not trade itself, as the central charge in the lament, and both read Tyre’s location on the sea and its commerce as the setting in which that pride grew.

verses.text: Your borders are in the heart of the seas. Your builders have perfected your beauty.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your borders are in the heart of the seas. Your builders have perfected your beauty.” The image of a ship now takes over, fitting for an island city whose strength was the sea. Arminian readers note that the beauty came from builders and materials, gifts and labor that Tyre treated as grounds for self-glory rather than stewardship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the poem quietly undercutting the boast of verse 3: Tyre said it was perfect, but others built its beauty. Shared ground: both traditions read the ship as an extended picture of the city’s wealth and security, and both see the image preparing for the wreck that follows in 27:26–36.

verses.text: They have made all your planks of cypress trees from Senir. They have taken a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you.
verses.arminianNotes: The ship’s planks are “of cypress trees from Senir,” and its mast is “a cedar from Lebanon.” Senir is another name for Mount Hermon (compare Deuteronomy 3:9). Arminian readers hear the choicest timber of the region gathered for Tyre’s use, a sign of how far its reach and influence extended among the peoples around it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same list as a portrait of borrowed glory: the finest woods of the north serve a city that claims its beauty as its own. Shared ground: both traditions read the materials as a celebration of skill and abundance that turns into a lament, since everything gathered here will sink with the ship.

verses.text: They have made your oars of the oaks of Bashan. They have made your benches of ivory inlaid in cypress wood from the islands of Kittim.
verses.arminianNotes: The oars are “of the oaks of Bashan,” and the benches are “of ivory inlaid in cypress wood from the islands of Kittim.” Kittim is often linked with Cyprus, though the name may cover a wider coastal region (compare Genesis 10:4). Arminian readers see luxury set even into the working parts of the ship, a picture of wealth spent on display.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the oaks of Bashan appear elsewhere among the lofty things the LORD brings low (compare Isaiah 2:13), and they hear that note here. Shared ground: both traditions read the ivory and fine woods as signs of extravagant prosperity, and both hold the identifications of distant places with some reserve.

verses.text: Your sail was of fine linen with embroidered work from Egypt, that it might be to you for a banner. Blue and purple from the islands of Elishah was your awning.
verses.arminianNotes: The sail is “of fine linen with embroidered work from Egypt,” serving as a banner, and the awning is “blue and purple from the islands of Elishah.” Elishah is possibly Cyprus or another coastal region to the west, but the identification is uncertain (compare Genesis 10:4). Arminian readers see Tyre advertising its splendor in every port it entered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the costly dyes and Egyptian linen as the dress of a city that clothed itself in the honors of the nations. Shared ground: both traditions read the sail as both practical and ornamental, a banner of status, and both see in it the self-display that the lament exposes; neither treats fine craftsmanship as sinful in itself.

verses.text: The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were your rowers. Your wise men, Tyre, were in you. They were your pilots.
verses.arminianNotes: “The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were your rowers.” Sidon lay north of Tyre, and Arvad is commonly identified with an island city farther north along the coast. Tyre’s own wise men served as pilots. Arminian readers see neighboring cities drawn into Tyre’s service, and a city confident in its own wisdom standing at the helm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the wisdom of Tyre’s pilots anticipates the theme of 28:3–5, where wisdom gained riches and riches lifted up the heart. Shared ground: both traditions read the crew as a picture of Tyre’s commanding place among the Phoenician cities, and both hear the stress on its own wisdom as part of the pride the LORD judges.

verses.text: The old men of Gebal and its wise men were your repairers of ship seams in you. All the ships of the sea with their mariners were in you to deal in your merchandise.
verses.arminianNotes: “The old men of Gebal and its wise men” repaired the ship’s seams. Gebal is commonly identified with the ancient port later known as Byblos. Every ship of the sea came to deal in Tyre’s merchandise. Arminian readers see skilled elders of other cities serving Tyre’s upkeep, and trade drawn into its orbit from every direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the picture of a hub toward which the commerce of the sea flowed, a center that seemed indispensable to the nations. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the description of Tyre’s greatness before its fall, and both note that the same mariners and repairers reappear in the wreck and the mourning of 27:27–29.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Persia, Lud, and Put were in your army, your men of war. They hung the shield and helmet in you. They showed your beauty.
verses.arminianNotes: “Persia, Lud, and Put were in your army.” Lud and Put are often associated with peoples in Asia Minor and North Africa, though the identifications are debated. These soldiers hung shield and helmet in the city. Arminian readers see Tyre relying on hired strength from distant lands, a security purchased with wealth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the foreign troops a further display of Tyre’s reach, and they note that the shields hung in the city “showed your beauty,” so that even its defense became ornament. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a confident, cosmopolitan power whose security would prove unable to save it (compare 27:27).

verses.text: The men of Arvad with your army were on your walls all around, and valiant men were in your towers. They hung their shields on your walls all around. They have perfected your beauty.
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Arvad stood on the walls, valiant men were in the towers, and their shields hung all around: “They have perfected your beauty.” Arminian readers note that the section ends where it began, with beauty, and they hear the repetition as the city’s own self-image reflected back to it in the poem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase framing verses 3–11 and setting up the reversal: the beauty that others perfected for Tyre will not keep it from ruin. Shared ground: both traditions read the shift here from ship to walled city as a natural blending of images for an island fortress, and both treat the passage as a picture of pride before a fall.
